title: Terms
text: One key + passphrase · Step 1 of 12 Terms ← Home Step 1 of 12 · Terms 2 · Before you begin → Time 10 min Difficulty Easy Steps 12 terms You will need: Nothing, just read The words you need before the work begins. Use these definitions as a reference throughout the guide. No secrets are needed to search. Find a term 12 terms shown. Seed phrase A human-readable backup used to derive wallet keys. Keep it secret. Recovery may also require a passphrase and, for multisig, the wallet configuration. Passphrase An additional secret used with a BIP39 seed phrase to derive a different wallet. The exact value matters: a typo can open a different, empty wallet. It is not the device PIN. Entropy Unpredictable input used to generate keys. Correct dice collection can provide entropy; it does not protect against malicious software that handles the result. BIP39 A specification for encoding entropy and a checksum as a mnemonic and deriving a seed from it, with an optional passphrase. It is more than a word list. Airgap Separation from networks. In this guide, secret-handling sessions use verified offline software. Turning networking off does not prove the computer is free of malware. Hash · file fingerprint A digest used to detect file changes. A match is useful only if the expected value comes from a trustworthy source; an attacker can replace both a file and its published hash. Digital signature A cryptographic check that a file was signed by a particular key and has not changed. Verify the signer’s key fingerprint independently; “Good signature” alone does not identify a trustworthy author. Extended public key · xpub Public information that can derive a branch of wallet addresses. It does not authorize spending on its own, but revealing it can expose wallet activity. Wallet descriptor A description of the scripts and public-key information used by a wallet. A watch-only descriptor is not a signing secret, but it is privacy-sensitive and important for multisig recovery. 2-of-3 multisig A wallet policy requiring signatures from two of three keys. Recovering with two seeds also needs the missing cosigner’s public information and the correct policy. PSBT Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction: a format for carrying transaction details and signatures between wallet software and signers. It can be used with single-signature and multisig wallets. Watch-only wallet A wallet holding public information so it can display addresses and transactions. It cannot sign by itself. Verify its receive addresses against independently trusted wallet details. Independent verification: two matching tools are not enough if both rely on the same compromised input. Check the source of the data as well as the result. Specifications: BIP39 · PSBT (BIP174) . ← Home ← Previous Home Step 1 of 12 2 · Before you begin → Next → Before you begin

title: Before you begin
text: One key + passphrase · Step 2 of 12 Before you begin ← 1 · Terms Step 2 of 12 · Before you begin 3 · Pick your path → Time 5 min Difficulty Easy Steps 1 worksheet You will need: Pen and paper What are you protecting your Bitcoin from? Two quick questions help you identify your risks. No secret keys or personal information are collected. 1 Choose your concerns ✓ Theft Someone gets access to a backup. ✓ Fire or flood A backup location is destroyed. ✓ Mistakes I lose or record something incorrectly. ✓ Scams Someone tricks me into sharing a secret. ✓ Inheritance My family needs to recover my Bitcoin. 2 Where is your Bitcoin today? On an exchange Someone else controls the keys. Phone or software wallet My keys are on an internet-connected device. Hardware wallet I already use a dedicated signing device. I haven't started I want to begin correctly. Your security priorities Select the risks you want to plan for, then choose where your Bitcoin is today. These choices help you think through risks; they do not automatically determine a safe wallet configuration. Choose your path → Explore wallet risks and tradeoffs One key and a passphrase Simpler to operate, but forgetting or losing the passphrase can permanently prevent recovery. A compromised device or poorly stored backup can still put funds at risk. Keep the passphrase on paper apart from the plate. If someone finds both the seed backup and its passphrase, they may be able to access your funds. Keep them separately and test restoration. One device, one maker. A flawed or tampered device can still fail you. Words and passphrase go into the device itself during recovery, nowhere else. No hardware company will ever ask for your seed phrase. Check the receiving address on the device screen, not only on the computer screen, before you accept coins. The watch-only wallet cannot sign. Spending requires the signing key for the passphrase-protected wallet; recovery requires the seed and the exact passphrase. A replacement compatible device can be used. Three keys (2-of-3 multisig) Separates signing keys across devices or locations, but makes setup and recovery more complicated. Securely preserve the wallet configuration/descriptor and test the recovery procedure. Most steps to get right. A missed step in any key can lock the wallet later. If fewer than two signing keys remain available, you cannot spend, even with the wallet map. Losing the map can also prevent recovery when the missing public-key information cannot be reconstructed. Keep three plates in three places, and keep the encrypted map apart from any single plate. Two signing keys meet the 2-of-3 threshold, but recovery also requires the correct wallet configuration. Keep verified copies of the descriptor and recovery instructions in separate safe locations, and rehearse reconstruction and spending before funding the wallet. No passphrase on the 2-of-3. The protection comes from three keys in three places, not from a passphrase. Use a disposable test wallet to practice spending and recovery for your chosen setup. Resolve failures before relying on an intended wallet; a practice transaction alone does not verify its backups. Shut down fully between keys. A key left in memory is a key at risk. Note: One stolen seed being insufficient applies to an appropriately configured 2-of-3 multisig, not all wallets. Multisig does not automatically solve scams, user error, coercion, or inheritance. Test recovery before trusting a wallet with meaningful funds. Never type seed phrases or passphrases into a website, form, or demo. ← 1 · Terms ← Previous Terms Step 2 of 12 3 · Pick your path → Next → Pick your path

title: Two boots
text: One key + passphrase · Step 5 of 12 Two boots ← 4 · Checklist Step 5 of 12 · Two boots 6 · Check the files → Time 45 min Difficulty Careful Steps 4 sections You will need: Everyday computer · Tails USB You will need for offline testing: Complete offline tester ZIP Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → Separate online preparation from offline secret handling. This page explains the session boundaries. Read Check the files and complete verification before installing or running downloaded software. Page order is not permission to skip that check. Limits: Tails and Offline Mode cannot make compromised hardware or firmware trustworthy. Reusing one computer for several keys creates shared risks that a reboot does not remove. Online preparation Download and verify first Follow the official Tails installation instructions for your computer and release. Authenticate the image before writing it. Keep a separate data USB for the specific verified files you need. Do not put seed phrases, raw entropy, private keys, or passphrases on the data USB or in the everyday operating system. Do not create or unlock Persistent Storage for this guide’s temporary secret-handling sessions. Offline session Set the boundary before secrets At the Tails Welcome Screen, enable Offline Mode before starting the desktop. Older instructions may call this networking disabled. Disconnect network cables and do not enable networking during the session. Use only the verified local tools required for the task. A webpage’s “offline” badge is a reminder, not proof of network isolation or a safe computer. One key or three? The one-key path creates one seed. The three-key path uses a separate session for each seed. Do not load multiple signing seeds in one session. Separate sessions reduce accidental mixing; they do not establish independent hardware trust. Transfer boundary Export only what the next step needs When the guide calls for a transfer, export only reviewed public wallet information or the required transaction file. Public descriptors and xpubs expose wallet activity and still need privacy protection. Never copy seeds, raw entropy, private-key exports, or secret-bearing wallet files back to the online computer. Do not assume a file is public because its name says “backup.” Inspect the export type and follow the wallet’s documentation. End the session Power off fully Finish the offline task and shut down Tails completely before another key session. Do not substitute suspend or hibernate. Keep your physical backup private, away from cameras and microphones. Shutdown ends the session; it does not undo a disclosure, erase a file you saved elsewhere, or remove malicious firmware. If isolation or software integrity is in doubt, stop and investigate before using that key. Stop if: verification is incomplete, networking was enabled while a secret was present, a secret was saved to transfer media, or you cannot identify what an export contains. Do not use a real funded wallet for a rehearsal. Official references: Welcome Screen and Offline Mode · Untrusted computer risks . Next, Check the files. Return to these session rules when the later steps require offline work. ← 4 · Checklist ← Previous Checklist Step 5 of 12 6 · Check the files → Next → Check the files

title: Check the files
text: One key + passphrase · Step 6 of 12 Check the files ← 5 · Two boots Step 6 of 12 · Check the files 7 · Make one key → Time About 30 min Approach One file at a time Checks Source · signer · contents Verification files at a glance Interactive controls are unavailable. All guided instructions are shown below. The software download: the file whose contents you check. Checksum list: the expected hashes; authenticate this list before relying on it. Signature: verify it over the named file or checksum list using the authenticated key. Publisher’s public key: confirm its full fingerprint independently. It is not your wallet seed or private key. Start with Guided checks , or explore the files and example outcomes. Diagrams and sample hashes explain the process; this page does not verify your downloads. 01 Guided checks One check at a time 02 Understand the files See what connects 03 Stop or continue? Explore the outcomes Check the files Start here Before you run it, know what you downloaded. A download needs more than a familiar logo. Answer three questions about each file before you use it. example-app.zip Start with one file Have these ready: your download, the project’s current verification instructions, and any verification files those instructions require. Choose a checkpoint to see the action, the reason, and what a pass means. 1 The right source? Find the exact project release. 2 The expected signer? Check the key and signature. 3 The same contents? Match your file to the reference. CHECKPOINT 1 / 3 Start at the project. Match your download. Use the project’s official instructions for your version and operating system. Keep that page open while you check. 1 Confirm the project’s domain through a source you already trust. Avoid ads and unsolicited download links. 2 Choose the release and platform you intend to use. 3 Save the download and its required verification files together. What this establishes You have identified the intended release. You still need the publisher and file-content checks. Follow the release, not the logo Project’s official instructions Confirm you have the right source ↓ select exact version + operating system Your download example-app.zip ↓ collect its required companions Verification files A signature, signed list, or project verifier File names here are examples. Each project supplies its own verification process. HTTPS protects the connection. It does not establish software safety. Next: check the signer → CHECKPOINT 2 / 3 Make sure the signature belongs to the right key. Use the publisher’s public verification key . This is separate from your wallet keys: file verification never needs your seed words or private keys. Establish whose key you expect, then check what it signed. 1 Follow the publisher’s documented process to confirm the signing key’s full fingerprint using an independently trusted source. 2 Use the project’s verifier or documented signature commands for the exact release. 3 Confirm the signature covers your download directly, or the checksum list that names your file. What this establishes A valid signature connects the signed content to the authenticated signing key. It does not audit the program’s code. Two checks that belong together Expected publisher’s key Full fingerprint independently confirmed ↓ use this key to verify Signature checks out For the download or its checksum list ↓ now you can use Authenticated signed content Compare the named file if a list was signed “Good signature” + unknown key is incomplete. A new key or unexplained fingerprint change needs investigation. No signature available? Use the publisher’s documented alternative. Do not treat an unsigned hash as publisher proof. Next: check your copy → CHECKPOINT 3 / 3 Compare your file with the expected hash. A SHA-256 hash is a 64-character digest of a file’s contents. Calculate yours and compare all 64 characters with the authenticated reference for that exact file. Windows macOS Linux Get-FileHash -LiteralPath ".\example-app.zip" -Algorithm SHA256 | Format-List PowerShell · run in the file’s folder, or use its full path Copy command What a match means Your file matches the referenced bytes. If the reference itself is unauthenticated, a match alone does not establish who published the file. If the publisher signs the download directly, follow its documented direct-signature process. A separate checksum list may not be required. Illustration only Show a mismatch Authenticated expected hash 9f3a18c7d42e6b508a9174c3e65f20b77dc58a014b2e939f6a70d1c84e5b6230 Calculated hash of your copy 9f3a18c7d42e6b508a9174c3e65f20b77dc58a014b2e939f6a70d1c84e5b6230 All 64 characters match These values are made-up teaching examples, not a checksum for a real download. Keep a record: filename, release, full hash, method, and key fingerprint where applicable. Explore stop / continue → Stop when something is unexplained. A wrong hash, failed signature, unknown key, or uncertain release needs investigation before you run the file. What if a signature checker reports an untrusted key? A valid signature and local key-trust settings answer different questions. “Not certified” may reflect your local trust configuration, but you still need to independently establish the key’s identity. Investigate an unexpected key, bad signature, or unresolved warning. Check the files · explain the pieces File roles Four files. Different jobs. The extra downloads can feel like clutter until you see what each one does. This example follows a project that publishes a signed checksum list. One release folder · select a file below to understand its role A example-app.zip The software you intend to use. B SHA256SUMS The expected hash for each release file. C SHA256SUMS.asc The signature for that checksum list. D publisher-key.asc The public key used to check the signature. This is the download you are checking. Calculate a hash from this file’s contents. Match it to the entry for this exact filename in the authenticated checksum list. What this file does not tell you Its name, icon, and successful download do not prove who published it. How the evidence connects Signed-list example 1 · Establish the reference Authenticated publisher key + Signature + checksum list ↓ Verify the signature over the list Expected hash from an authenticated list Confirm the key fingerprint independently first. 2 · Examine your copy Your downloaded example-app.zip + A SHA-256 calculation tool ↓ Calculate the digest of your copy Calculated hash for the downloaded file Use a trusted tool, following the project’s instructions. AUTHENTICATED EXPECTED HASH ↔ YOUR CALCULATED HASH Same filename. Same release. Every character. A full match links your copy to the authenticated reference. A mismatch means stop and investigate. Some projects sign the download directly. In that case, verify the signature over the downloaded file using the authenticated key. Use the publisher’s actual filenames and instructions; the four filenames above are examples. Check the files · see the outcome Example outcomes Know when to stop. Know what to do next. Explore four sample results. The decision map shows exactly where a verification attempt needs more work. Everything lines up All checks established Only the hash matches Reference not authenticated “Good signature” Signer’s identity unknown One character differs Calculated hash mismatch Example verification path 1 Right source, file, and release? YES · continue ↓ 2 Expected key identity established? YES · continue ↓ 3 Signature over the list valid? YES · continue ↓ 4 Your file’s hash matches its entry? YES · continue ↓ RECORD THE FILE-CHECK RESULT Selected scenario The file checks line up. You identified the release, independently authenticated the publisher key, verified its signature on the checksum list, and matched the entire hash for your file. File checks complete for this example Record what you checked. This establishes the file’s connection to the authenticated release reference. What you do next Keep the filename, release, full hash, method, and key fingerprint in your verification record. Continue only when the guide’s other release and testing requirements are also satisfied. This map illustrates a signed checksum list. A project’s direct-file signature or dedicated verification tool may use a different route. A successful file check does not establish that software is bug-free or approved for custody. Current instructions always come from the project: Tails installation ↗ Sparrow verification ↗ Public test site: the tools and instructions remain under review. Never enter signing secrets into the live website. Successful file checks do not certify software safety or approve a custody release. Testing Plebum Dominium’s own downloads? For public-fixture testing: use the manifest and instructions supplied with your exact package version. You will need for offline testing: Fingerprint checker · ZIP checksums Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → A package checksum checks consistency with its reference; it does not independently audit code or establish publisher identity. Review and authenticate any verification script before running it. Keep a verification record: release, exact filename, full hash, method, and signing-key fingerprint when applicable. Verify every required file before beginning your path’s offline secret-handling session. ← 5 · Two boots ← Previous Two boots Step 6 of 12 7 · Make one key → Next → Make one key

title: Make one key
text: One key + passphrase · Step 7 of 12 Make one key ← 6 · Check the files Step 7 of 12 · Make one key 8 · Back up your key → Time 30-45 min Difficulty Moderate Steps 6 sections You will need: 5 dice · Paper and pen · The worksheet You will need for offline testing: Dice converter HTML · Python dice converter Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → You will roll dice to create one Bitcoin seed phrase. Each one becomes 24 words. The computer never sees the network while you work. Safety first: Never enter seed words on an online computer. Boot Tails with networking Disabled before you start. Shut down fully between each key. What you will do Boot Tails offline. Copy the dice converter page. Roll dice. Enter the faces. The page counts to 256 bits. Write down the 24 words. Prove them with a second tool. Shut down after checking the one seed. Do not create additional seeds for this path. Step 1 / 6 Boot Tails. Copy the converter. Boot Tails with networking set to Disabled. Copy the checked dice converter page from the data USB to the Desktop. Check: Open only the verified local copy after enabling Tails Offline Mode. An offline indicator alone does not prove network isolation. If it reports online, stop. Step 2 / 6 Roll the dice. Enter the faces. Roll five dice at once. Enter each face as you roll it. Using fair, independently rolled dice and a fixed reading order, faces 1 to 4 count as bits (1=00, 2=01, 3=10, 4=11). Faces 5 and 6 are skipped, roll those dice again. The page counts the pairs and stops you at 128. SHAKE 1 SHAKE 2 SHAKE 3 11 RE-ROLL 01 00 10 01 01 RE-ROLL 11 11 00 10 00 10 RE-ROLL 00 01 RE-ROLL 10 256-BIT STRING 11 00 10 01 01 01 11 00 10 11 00 10 00 01 10 …keep rolling… 256 / 256 BITS 10 / 256 20 / 256 30 / 256 256 / 256 24 WORDS Roll as many times as needed to get 256 bits of entropy: about 39 shakes. Check: The page shows 128 pairs and 256 bits. Count accepted pairs, not an estimated number of shakes. Step 3 / 6 Write the 24 words. At 256 bits the page prints 24 words. In a 24-word BIP39 phrase, the last word contains three entropy bits and eight checksum bits. It is not an arbitrary check word: never invent or alter it. Write all 24 on the grid. Compare them privately in order, away from cameras and microphones. Check: All 24 words and their positions are recorded accurately; a valid checksum does not prove safe randomness. Step 4 / 6 Prove it with a second tool. Use a separately verified offline implementation with the exact same 256-bit entropy and BIP39 settings. Raw dice inputs are not interchangeable between tools: some hash the roll string while this guide maps accepted faces to bit pairs. Confirm the input method before comparing all 24 words. If you cannot establish that the inputs and method match, stop; do not guess or choose a preferred output. Check: Both tools show the same 24 words. Step 5 / 6 Finish the one-key session. Finish checking the one seed, then shut Tails down fully. Keep its backup private. This path does not require a second or third signing seed. Check: One seed is recorded on one numbered grid. No additional signing seeds are needed. Step 6 / 6 Confirm the checks agree. The checksum detects many transcription errors, but not all of them. It does not authenticate the source of the words. At least two checks must agree: the two tools showing the same words, and the wallet (Sparrow or Electrum, offline) opening the list without error. If anything disagrees, stop. Stop if: The page says online. The two tools show different words. The wallet rejects the list. Any of these means stop and start that key over. Next, back up your key using the next page on this path. ← 6 · Check the files ← Previous Check the files Step 7 of 12 8 · Back up your key → Next → Back up your key

title: Back up your key
text: One key + passphrase · Step 8 of 12 Stamp the plate ← 7 · Make one key Step 8 of 12 · Back up your key 9 · If I am gone → Make a durable backup without losing the ability to recover. Record accurately Back up the one seed using the chosen medium’s instructions. Preserve word order and any required encoding information. Work privately and compare every entry against the original. Keep the original protected while checking the replacement. A damaged or ambiguous mark needs correction before you rely on it. Check recovery safely Use the wallet’s documented backup-check or recovery procedure on trusted equipment. Do not wipe your only working signer to test an unproven backup. Never type seeds into this website or an online form. For a rehearsal, use a disposable test wallet. For an existing funded wallet, plan the verification carefully before changing devices or backups. Keep the complete recovery information Record the wallet software, network, script type, account and derivation path. Preserve a verified public descriptor if your wallet supports exporting one. The exact passphrase is a separate recovery secret, not a device PIN. A different passphrase selects a different wallet. Store a durable, accurate record separately from the seed backup. Plan copies and locations Balance loss, theft, access, and disaster risks. More copies can improve availability and also expose secrets in more places. Document which locations contain which material; do not combine enough signing secrets in one place to defeat your separation plan. Do not destroy an original merely because a new backup looks correct. Retire it only after a successful recovery check and a deliberate review of the remaining copies. Revisit the plan when locations or helpers change. Stop if: a backup is unreadable, the recovered wallet differs, or any required passphrase or configuration is missing. Do not overwrite or discard the remaining working material. ← 7 · Make one key ← Previous Make one key Step 8 of 12 9 · If I am gone → Next → If I am gone

title: If I am gone
text: One key + passphrase · Step 9 of 12 If I am gone Choose a path One device One key + passphrase Three keys ← 8 · Back up your key Step 9 of 12 · If I am gone 10 · If you get stuck → Help a trusted person understand what to find—and when to stop. Leave a clear private plan Describe the wallet type, the location of the full instructions, the required recovery items, and a trusted contact who can explain the process. Keep signing secrets out of this website, email, and the general instruction sheet. Separate ownership and access arrangements from the technical recovery instructions. Make sure the intended person can find the plan when needed. Identify the required items This path requires the seed backup and the exact wallet passphrase. Record the wallet software, network, script type, account and derivation path. Preserve a verified public descriptor if your wallet supports exporting one. The passphrase cannot be reset by a wallet company. A wallet opened without it, or with a typo, may show a different balance. Do not assume that balance represents all of the owner’s funds. Confirm the recovered wallet Follow the recorded, rehearsed procedure and verify the policy and wallet details against independent trusted records. An address match alone does not establish that a coordinator is trustworthy. If the wallet is empty or differs from the records, stop. Check the passphrase, account, network, derivation information and synchronization before concluding funds are lost. Do not overwrite backups or create replacement keys as a guess. Practice before an emergency Walk through locating the records and explaining the steps with the intended helper. Use a disposable test wallet for hands-on training, without exposing the owner’s signing secrets. When a legitimate recovery is needed, independently verify the destination and transaction details on trusted signing equipment. A small successful transfer is useful evidence, but it is not a complete audit of the recovery setup. Protect the secrets: no legitimate support agent needs a seed phrase or private key. If the instructions, equipment compatibility, or wallet identity are uncertain, stop before entering secrets or signing. ← 8 · Back up your key ← Previous Back up your key Step 9 of 12 10 · If you get stuck → Next → If you get stuck

title: If you get stuck
text: One key + passphrase · Step 10 of 12 If you get stuck ← 9 · If I am gone Step 10 of 12 · If you get stuck 11 · Recovery card → Find the problem, preserve what still works, and stop when the next step is uncertain. What setup is this? This route uses one signing seed and an exact wallet passphrase, backed up separately. A replacement compatible signer can recover it; the original device is not an additional required secret. What recovery information matters? The seed and exact passphrase select the intended wallet. Preserve the configuration too. A different passphrase selects a different wallet; it does not add a password to funds already held elsewhere. The download or version does not match Stop before running it. Confirm the exact release, file, signature and full hash from the intended publisher. Do not assume a newer release is compatible or an older release is safe. The staging download inventory has unresolved mismatches; see Downloads . The two converters disagree Preserve the original rolls privately. Check transcription, input method, bit order and settings. Do not guess a replacement word or choose whichever output you prefer. Use public test vectors before trusting the procedure; funded-wallet backups must not be edited to make a check pass. The restored wallet looks empty Stop before wiping or discarding anything. Check the network, account, script type, derivation settings, passphrase if used, and synchronization. Preserve working devices and backups while investigating. Never send secrets to someone offering recovery help. Where should secrets be kept? Keep signing secrets offline and protected from theft and loss. Avoid photographs, email, cloud notes and online forms. Plan durable copies and separate locations, then test recovery. A location card is not a substitute for the backups. How can a helper prepare? Practice with a disposable wallet and a private written plan. Use the recovery planning guide where it matches your wallet. Never paste real seeds, passwords or passphrases into this site. ← 9 · If I am gone ← Previous If I am gone Step 10 of 12 11 · Recovery card → Next → Recovery card

title: Recovery card
text: One key + passphrase · Step 11 of 12 Recovery card ← 10 · If you get stuck Step 11 of 12 · Recovery card 12 · One key + passphrase → A private pointer to your recovery plan—not a wallet backup. What this card is for A short location record helps an authorized person find the complete instructions and required materials. It cannot replace the seed backup and the exact wallet passphrase. Location information can help a thief too. Protect the card even though it contains no signing secrets. Write these pointers offline Wallet type: one key + passphrase. Where to find the complete recovery instructions. Seed-backup location and separate passphrase-record location. Trusted contact and date last reviewed. Location of any separate decryption instructions, if required. Write privately on paper. This page intentionally provides no form for entering real locations or secrets. Never include these No seed words, raw entropy, private keys, wallet passphrases, or decryption passwords on the card. Keep it separate from the materials it points to. A descriptor can contain private keys; only a verified public-only export belongs in the non-signing configuration records. Keep it current Check that the intended person can follow the pointers. Update the record after moving a backup or changing the recovery plan, then account for obsolete copies. The downloadable legacy card/PDF has not yet been reconciled with these revised instructions. Do not treat that older packet as a verified version of this page. Recovery still requires verification: use the complete, rehearsed procedure. A list of locations, a device brand, or a derivation-path label is not sufficient by itself. ← 10 · If you get stuck ← Previous If you get stuck Step 11 of 12 12 · One key + passphrase → Next → One key + passphrase

title: One key + passphrase
text: One key + passphrase · Step 12 of 12 One key, done right You will need for offline testing: Diceware mapper · EFF wordlist Save these files before disconnecting. Public test data only; tools remain under review. Full offline kit and instructions → ← 11 · Recovery card Step 12 of 12 · One key + passphrase Review this path → Finish the one-key and passphrase plan without risking your only working wallet. 1. Assess the existing wallet If funds are on an exchange, you may not control its signing keys. If a seed may be exposed, plan a move to a newly generated wallet. Preserve the old working signer and records until the transfer and recovery checks are complete. Do not overwrite its seed in place. 2. Prepare the new signer Use compatible equipment and follow its official setup and recovery instructions. For this route choose a device that supports entering your secrets on the device itself. Verify its provenance and software; a brand name or intact seal is not a complete security check. Use the one-key generation guide only after its prerequisites and input-method checks are satisfied. 3. Understand the passphrase Adding a passphrase selects a separate wallet. It does not move existing funds or protect coins left in the previous wallet. Use a strong independently generated passphrase, record it exactly and keep durable backups separate from the seed. Check the device’s character and length limits. 4. Verify recovery before funding Keep the seed, exact passphrase and wallet configuration recoverable. Use the documented backup-check method; do not wipe your only working signer to test an unproven backup. Investigate unexpected addresses or balances without destroying the original records. See backup checks . 5. Connect and transfer carefully Export public information to the watch-only coordinator. Verify the intended receive address on the trusted device before sending a small first transfer. Confirm receipt and practice signing, checking destination, amount, fee and change. Plan further transfers only after the recovery checks pass. 6. Keep the plan maintainable Do not destroy old backups just because one account displays zero; other accounts, pending payments or future incoming transfers may still matter. Document retirement deliberately. A decoy balance is not guaranteed protection under coercion. Prepare a private recovery plan for trusted helpers. ← 11 · Recovery card ← Previous Recovery card Step 12 of 12 Review this path → Next → Review this path

title: Chainalysis restores key services after credential exposure
text: Latest update Updated November 7, 2026 Chainalysis restores key services after credential exposure Chainalysis said on November 7 that Reactor, KYT and Address Screening were back online with additional security measures. The restoration follows a broader disclosure on November 4: names, usernames, password hashes and active access tokens for all users had been exposed. A separate attack also exposed some customer passwords. The company took products offline and notified customers whose KYT accounts appeared to have been accessed without permission. Its recovery instructions call for password resets and API-key rotation where applicable. In its November 4 update, Chainalysis said it had found no evidence that investigation data had been accessed or its address-attribution data altered. That is a statement about the evidence available at that time. Why it matters here Security providers can be breached too. Use a different password for each service, open the known website yourself when checking a security notice, and keep wallet recovery words out of support messages and online accounts. Restored service does not undo information already exposed. Source: Chainalysis incident updates, November 4–7

title: Binance confirms $6.34 billion theft and publishes initial findings
text: Updated report Incident October 29 · Report November 3, 2026 Binance confirms $6.34 billion theft and publishes initial findings Binance has confirmed the October 29 theft. In its November 3 preliminary report, the exchange put the affected assets at about $6.34 billion and said about $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted. It said it had reserved enough company funds to cover the loss and replenished 98% of the affected token assets. Those figures are Binance’s report for that date; frozen assets are not the same as funds returned. Binance said attackers gained unauthorized access to an internal wallet-signing service. Its account describes compromised employee devices, malicious downloads and fake recruitment interviews. The company said it rebuilt affected systems and was commissioning independent security reviews. Its findings remain preliminary. Why it matters here The practical lesson is to protect the whole signing process: the software you download, the computer you use and the details you approve. A promise to cover an exchange loss still depends on that company. Self-custody transfers responsibility to you, so practice setup, signing and recovery before relying on a wallet. Source: Binance preliminary findings, November 3

title: Mercado Bitcoin theft: investigators estimate $49 million stolen
text: November 2, 2026 Mercado Bitcoin theft: investigators estimate $49 million stolen Chainalysis, which helped respond to the November 2 attack on Brazil’s Mercado Bitcoin exchange, estimated that about $49 million was stolen across 17 blockchains. It said its work with law enforcement and asset issuers helped freeze nearly $10 million. The company was still tracing the remaining funds when it published its report. Why it matters here Tracing stolen coins can help an investigation, but it does not guarantee their return. Some centrally issued tokens can be frozen by their issuers; Bitcoin has no equivalent issuer-operated freeze. Verify the receiving address and transaction details before signing. Recovery after a theft is uncertain. Source: Chainalysis incident response report, November 2

title: Coinbase vendor breach exposes customer contact data
text: October 2026 Coinbase vendor breach exposes customer contact data On October 27, 2026, Coinbase said a security incident at Amplitude, a third-party analytics vendor, exposed contact and limited transaction data for a small subset of its customers. Coinbase said its own systems were not breached and customer funds were not affected. The company did not say how many customers were affected or which fields were taken. A claim on X that more than 70,000 users were affected was called false by Coinbase. The company is notifying affected customers and regulators. Why it matters here An exchange can keep your coins safe and still leak your contact details through a vendor you never chose. That data is what makes phishing convincing: a message that knows your name, your phone number, and your recent transactions. Treat any message claiming to be from an exchange as suspect until you verify it through a channel you opened yourself. Keep your seed material entirely off any system tied to an exchange account. Sources: Unchained · CoinDesk · Cointelegraph

title: Keystone breach exposes customer shipping addresses
text: October 2026 Keystone breach exposes customer shipping addresses On October 24, 2026, Keystone disclosed a website breach that exposed customer shipping data, including home addresses tied to past hardware wallet orders. The company said private keys and funds on its devices were not affected, since that material never touches the internet. Keystone has not said how many customers were affected or how the breach happened. Why it matters here A shipping address tied to a hardware wallet order tells a thief where a holder lives, which enables physical targeting and phishing that references your real order. This guide tells you to buy devices from the maker’s own shop. Ship those orders to an address that is not your home, and treat any message about your order as suspect. Sources: AltcoinDaily

title: State Bank of India: 3,897 customer records on the dark web
text: October 2026 State Bank of India: 3,897 customer records on the dark web On October 21, 2026, State Bank of India disclosed an incident involving customer data on the dark web. The bank said it was alerted on October 16 by its threat intelligence provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and CERT-In. A preliminary analysis of about 375,000 records found 3,897 customer records containing personal information. Those records included names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and customer identifiers, and loan and lead metadata. The bank said customer balances were completely safe, that the incident had no material impact on core operations, and that it had engaged an independent CERT-In empanelled agency for a full assessment. Why it matters here A bank can keep balances safe and still leak your home address, your phone number, and your loan history. That is the data used for targeted phishing and for physical targeting. Treat any message claiming to be from a bank or an exchange as suspect until you verify it through a separate channel you trust, and keep your plates, your map, and your passphrase paper in separate places, away from anything tied to that leaked identity data. Sources: Reuters · The Hindu BusinessLine

title: South Korea: hacking incidents at seven banks linked to one attacker
text: October 2026 South Korea: hacking incidents at seven banks linked to one attacker On October 4, 2026, South Korean financial authorities said hacking incidents at seven financial institutions appeared to be linked to the same attacker. The institutions named were Shinhan, KB Kookmin, Hana, BNK Busan Bank, Yeogaram, Welcome Savings Bank, and Hyundai Capital. Authorities shared the attacker's internet addresses and security precautions with about 500 firms in the sector and started urgent inspections. At Shinhan, information leaked through a system used by employees and loan recruiters. Customer internet and mobile banking were not affected, and no financial losses were reported there. Authorities grouped the incidents into information inquiry services, employee support services, and website services. Why it matters here The entry point was not the main customer banking system. It was employee and recruiter systems around it. That is a reason not to trust a large institution to protect every piece of your identity data, and a reason to keep seed material out of any system tied to a bank, a loan application, or an employer portal. Your plates and your map do not belong in the same place as your banking identity. Sources: Aju Press · Tech Insider

title: Two hardware failures in one year
text: October 2026 Two hardware failures in one year In July 2026, attackers drained about 1,816 bitcoin from more than 5,200 Coldcard wallets. The cause was a firmware flaw from March 2021 that left some seeds with as little as 40 bits of real randomness instead of 128. Updating the firmware did not fix seeds already made. Owners had to move their funds to new seeds. In October 2026, Ledger confirmed an unauthorized hardware implant in at least one device sold by the Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis. Researchers estimate $86 million to $93 million was taken from hundreds of wallets. Ledger said its own systems and direct sales were not affected, and every confirmed case so far traces to that reseller. Why it matters here Both failures break the same promise: that the device can be trusted on its own. The guide answers that three ways. Buy from the maker’s own shop, never a reseller and never a used device. Never let a device roll its own entropy: make the seed with dice on an offline boot, then import it. And for a single key, require a passphrase: researchers noted that seeds made with dice rolls or protected by a strong passphrase were not the ones drained. A device you trust less is a device you verify more. Sources: Decrypt · CoinDesk

title: Russia closes the exchange off-ramp
text: October 2026 Russia closes the exchange off-ramp Russia’s new digital-asset law (No. 282-FZ, in force since September 1) routes all crypto buying through licensed brokers and state-approved banks. The central bank’s October guidance is explicit: moving crypto from a regulated account to your own wallet is not permitted, and peer-to-peer trades between individuals end entirely on July 1, 2027. Small buyers are capped at roughly $3,800 a year: bitcoin, ether, or tether only. Nobody banned holding your own keys. They closed the door between the regulated system and self-custody. That door is the exact step this guide starts with, when you withdraw a test amount from an exchange to an address only you control. Why it matters here Rules can close an off-ramp at any time, in any country. A wallet built before you need it never has to ask permission. Build it while the door is open. Sources: Cointelegraph · TFTC

title: Coinbase: bribed support agents leak data on 69,461 customers
text: May 2025 Coinbase: bribed support agents leak data on 69,461 customers On May 15, 2025, Coinbase disclosed that criminals had bribed overseas customer support agents to steal customer data. The siphoning began on December 26, 2024 and was detected on May 11, 2025, when the attackers demanded a $20 million ransom. A later filing put the number at 69,461 customers, less than 1% of monthly transacting users. The stolen data included names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, the last four digits of Social Security numbers, masked bank details, government ID images, and account balances and transaction histories. Passwords, private keys, and customer funds were not taken. Coinbase refused the ransom, offered a $20 million reward for information leading to arrests, and estimated remediation and reimbursements at $180 million to $400 million. Why it matters here This is the insider version of the same lesson. The attackers did not break the cryptography. They paid the people who answer the phones. An exchange holds your name, your home address, your ID, and your transaction history in systems its own contractors can read. That data enabled phishing that tricked some customers into sending coins to scammers. Self-custody removes the coins from that database. It does not remove your identity from it, which is why the guide keeps seed material off every system tied to an exchange account. Sources: SecurityWeek · TechStory

title: FTX collapses, $8 billion in customer funds missing
text: November 2022 FTX collapses, $8 billion in customer funds missing FTX was one of the largest crypto exchanges in the world, valued at $32 billion in early 2022. On November 2, 2022, CoinDesk published the balance sheet of Alameda Research, the trading firm run by the same people, and it showed billions in FTT, a token FTX had printed itself. Customers rushed to withdraw. About $6 billion left in 72 hours, and the money was not there. FTX halted withdrawals on November 8 and filed for bankruptcy on November 11, revealing a shortfall of roughly $8 billion in customer funds. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted on seven fraud and conspiracy counts in November 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in March 2024. The bankruptcy estate later repaid most customers in dollars, but priced at November 2022 values, so a customer who had held one bitcoin got back the dollar value of a bitcoin on the day the company failed, not the bitcoin. Why it matters here An exchange balance is a claim on a company, not money in your pocket. The moment withdrawals stop, that distinction becomes the whole story. This guide keeps no balance anywhere: you buy, you withdraw a test amount to an address only you control, and you verify it before the rest follows. Even a bankruptcy that pays everyone back in dollars can still take your bitcoin. Sources: Nasdaq · Wikipedia

title: Ledger breach exposes 272,000 customer addresses
text: July 2020 Ledger breach exposes 272,000 customer addresses Ledger makes hardware wallets, and in July 2020 it disclosed that an attacker had reached its e-commerce and marketing database through a third party API key. At first Ledger said about 9,500 customers had detailed records exposed, alongside more than one million email addresses. In December 2020 the full database appeared on a public forum, and the real count was about 272,000 detailed records: names, postal addresses, and phone numbers of people who had ordered a device. No keys and no funds were touched. The damage was different: years of phishing emails and texts aimed at recovery phrases, SIM swaps, and extortion threats, all aimed at people whose home addresses were now in criminal hands. Ledger later confirmed that rogue members of its e-commerce provider’s support team had also exported customer records in April and June 2020. Why it matters here Order data is physical security data. A home address tied to a hardware wallet order tells a criminal what you own and where you keep it, and that data stays dangerous for years after the breach. Order from the maker’s shop, ship to an address that is not your home, and treat any message about your order as suspect. Sources: Ledger · CoinDesk

title: QuadrigaCX dies with its founder, $190 million locked away
text: January 2019 QuadrigaCX dies with its founder, $190 million locked away QuadrigaCX was Canada’s largest crypto exchange when its founder, Gerald Cotten, died in India in December 2018 at age 30. He alone held the passwords to the company’s cold wallets. His widow had his encrypted laptop and no password, and no one else at the company could open the wallets. About 115,000 customers were owed roughly $190 million. The exchange filed for bankruptcy in April 2019. In June 2020, Ontario’s securities regulator concluded the operation had been a fraud and a Ponzi scheme, with Cotten trading against customers under aliases. Whether the keys were truly lost or never existed, the result for customers was the same: the money was gone. Why it matters here One person holding every key is the failure this guide is built to remove. A 2-of-3 spread across three keys and three places survives any single death, loss, or theft, and the inheritance sheet exists so the people you trust can still open the fund when you cannot. Sources: CoinDesk · Wikipedia

title: Mt. Gox loses 850,000 bitcoin
text: February 2014 Mt. Gox loses 850,000 bitcoin Mt. Gox was the world’s largest bitcoin exchange, handling more than 70 percent of all bitcoin transactions in early 2014. On February 24, 2014, it suspended trading and went offline. Four days later it filed for bankruptcy in Tokyo, admitting about 850,000 bitcoin had gone missing, worth roughly $450 million at the time. About 200,000 were later recovered from an old wallet. The rest were never found. Investigations later showed the exchange had been losing coins to attackers since 2011, slowly, through flaws in how it tracked withdrawals. Creditors waited a decade: repayments through Kraken and Bitstamp began in July 2024, and the deadline for the remaining distributions runs to October 31, 2026. Why it matters here This is the original lesson of the site. Coins left on an exchange are the exchange’s coins until you withdraw them, and no reputation or size changes that. The practice spend exists so you prove the withdrawal step with a small amount before your savings ever move. Sources: The Block · Wikipedia
